content: Nutritional rickets is a condition that affects growing children, leading to bone deformities, bone pain, seizures, or delays in motor development. Currently, the disease is most prevalent in low-income countries. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions in preventing nutritional rickets in children born at term. The research involved a systematic search of databases such as The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, as well as reviewing reference lists of relevant articles. Authors of studies and reviews were contacted to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria required studies to be randomized controlled trials, controlled clinical trials, or prospective cohort studies that compared any intervention for preventing nutritional rickets in term-born children against a placebo or no intervention. The minimum duration of the intervention was set at three months for children under 12 months of age and six months for children over 12 months. Data extraction and quality assessment were conducted independently by two authors. Missing information was obtained by contacting the authors of the included studies. Four studies, involving approximately 1,700 participants, were included in the analysis. The duration of these trials ranged from nine months to two years. Three of the studies were randomized controlled trials, two of which used a cluster-randomized design. One study appeared to be a controlled trial with researcher-determined group assignments. In children up to three years of age in Turkey, supplementation with vitamin D compared to no intervention resulted in a relative risk of 0.04 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0 to 0.71), indicating a significant reduction in the risk of rickets. In a Chinese trial involving children up to three years of age, a combined intervention consisting of vitamin D supplementation, calcium supplementation, and nutritional counseling showed a relative risk of 0.76 (95% CI: 0.61 to 0.95) compared to no intervention, despite notable non-compliance among participants. In two studies conducted in older children in China and France, no cases of rickets were observed in either the intervention or control groups. The authors concluded that there is a limited number of studies on the prevention of nutritional rickets in term-born children. Until more data become available, it is reasonable to recommend preventive measures, such as vitamin D or calcium supplementation, for high-risk groups. These groups include infants and toddlers, children living in Africa, Asia, or the Middle East, and children who have migrated from these regions to areas where rickets is uncommon. However, due to significant clinical variability and the limited amount of data, further research is needed to evaluate the primary and adverse effects of preventive measures against nutritional rickets across different countries, age groups, and ethnic populations.
